title: Characteristics of Sound — Previous Board Question, 2017; adapted
question: A student must identify the physical factors primarily associated with loudness, pitch and quality of a musical note. Which sequence is correct?

options.text: Frequency, amplitude, speed of sound
Amplitude, frequency, waveform and relative strengths of overtones
Wavelength, speed of sound, amplitude
Quality, frequency, wavelength

explanation: Loudness is associated with intensity and amplitude; pitch is associated primarily with frequency; quality or timbre depends on waveform and harmonic content. Sound speed is not the defining factor for these three characteristics.

title: Echo Between Two Cliffs — Previous Board Question, 2015; adapted
question: A person stands 480 m from the nearer of two cliffs and shouts. The first echo is heard after 3 s, and the second echo is heard 2 s after the first. Assuming the sound travels at a constant speed, what are the speed of sound and the distance between the person and the farther cliff?

options.text: 160 m/s and 800 m
320 m/s and 960 m
320 m/s and 800 m
330 m/s and 990 m

explanation:
The first echo travels to the nearer cliff and back:


v=(2(480) / 3)=320 m/s


The second echo arrives 3+2=5 s after the shout. Thus,


d_{far}=(vt / 2)
=frac{320(5)}2=800 m


The time given for the second echo is measured from the original shout, not from the first echo.

title: Resonance of Pendulums — Previous Board Question, 2015; adapted
question: Four pendulums hang from a common elastic support. Pendulums P and R have equal lengths; Q is shorter than P, and S is longer than P. When P is set oscillating, which pendulum is expected to undergo the largest forced-vibration amplitude under suitable low-damping conditions?

options.text: R, because its natural frequency matches that of P
Q, because a shorter pendulum always resonates more strongly
S, because a longer pendulum always receives more energy
All four, because they share the same support

explanation: Pendulums of equal length have equal natural frequencies. R therefore has the best frequency match with P and can undergo resonance, whereas Q and S have different natural frequencies.

title: String Frequency — Previous Board Question, 2017; adapted
question: A stretched wire of length 80 cm has a fundamental frequency of 256 Hz. A similar wire under the same tension and with the same linear density is shortened to one-quarter of its original length. Its fundamental frequency becomes:

options.text: 64 Hz
512 Hz
256 Hz

explanation:
For a stretched string under constant tension and linear density,


fproptofrac1L


Reducing the length to one-quarter makes the frequency four times as great:


f₂=4(256)=1024 Hz

title: Sound and Light — Previous Board Question, 2010; adapted
question: Which combination correctly distinguishes sound waves in air from light waves?

options.text: Both require a material medium and both are longitudinal.
Sound requires a material medium and is longitudinal in air; light can travel through a vacuum and is transverse.
Sound can travel through a vacuum, but light cannot.
Both can travel through a vacuum, but only sound is transverse.

explanation: Sound is a mechanical wave and needs a medium. Light is an electromagnetic wave and can travel through a vacuum. Sound in air is longitudinal, while light is transverse.

title: Amplitude and Loudness — Previous Board Question, 2010; adapted
question: Two sound waves of equal frequency have amplitudes in the ratio 2:3. Assuming comparable conditions in the same medium, the ratio of their intensities is:
explanation:
Intensity is proportional to the square of amplitude:


I₁:I₂=2²:3²=4:9


Their frequencies are equal, so the waves have the same pitch; the larger-amplitude wave has greater intensity.

title: Free and Forced Vibrations — Previous Board Question, 2023; adapted
question: A body vibrates under a periodic external force. Which statement best identifies the nature of its vibrations while the external force continues to act?

options.text: They are always free vibrations because the body has its own natural frequency.
They are necessarily damped vibrations because energy is always lost.
They are always resonant vibrations, irrespective of the driving frequency.
They are forced vibrations, and resonance occurs when the driving frequency matches the natural frequency under suitable conditions.

explanation: An ongoing periodic external force produces forced vibrations. Resonance is a special case of forced vibration in which the driving frequency matches the system's natural frequency.

title: Damped Vibrations — Previous Board Question, 2017; adapted
question: A metal ruler clamped to a table is displaced at its free end and released. Its oscillations gradually become smaller. Which explanation is correct?

options.text: The oscillations are damped because energy is dissipated to the surroundings.
The oscillations are forced because the table supplies a periodic force.
The oscillations are undamped because the ruler continues moving.
The oscillations stop because their frequency must become zero immediately.

explanation:
is correct?

A) The oscillations are damped because energy is dissipated to the surroundings.
B) The oscillations are forced because the table supplies a periodic force.
C) The oscillations are undamped because the ruler continues moving.
D) The oscillations stop because their frequency must become zero immediately.

**Correct Answer: A**

**Reason:** Air resistance and internal friction dissipate mechanical energy, causing the amplitude to decrease. This is the characteristic behaviour of damped vibrations.

title: Resonance Tube — Previous Board Question, 2024; adapted
question: A tuning fork is held above the mouth of a tube containing an adjustable air column. At a particular length, the sound becomes markedly louder. What is the best explanation?

options.text: The air column has increased the tuning fork's frequency.
The speed of sound becomes infinite at the resonant length.
The natural frequency of the air column matches the tuning fork's frequency, producing resonance.
The air column absorbs all sound except the tuning fork's fundamental frequency.

explanation:
?

A) The air column has increased the tuning fork's frequency.
B) The speed of sound becomes infinite at the resonant length.
C) The natural frequency of the air column matches the tuning fork's frequency, producing resonance.
D) The air column absorbs all sound except the tuning fork's fundamental frequency.

**Correct Answer: C**

**Reason:** At resonance, the air column responds strongly because its natural frequency matches the tuning fork's frequency. For a closed air column, changing the length changes its resonant frequencies.

title: SONAR — Previous Board Question, 2024; adapted
question: Which type of wave is used by SONAR to detect underwater objects and determine depth?

options.text: Audible sound waves only
Ultrasonic waves
Radio waves travelling through seawater
Visible light waves

explanation: SONAR commonly uses ultrasonic sound pulses. The time taken for a pulse to travel to an underwater object and return is used to determine its distance.

title: Combined Wave-Property Trap
question: A sound source in air is replaced with another source producing twice the frequency and three times the amplitude. The air temperature and composition remain unchanged. Which set of changes is correct?

options.text: Speed doubles, wavelength remains unchanged, intensity triples.
Speed remains unchanged, wavelength doubles, intensity increases ninefold.
Speed remains unchanged, wavelength halves, intensity increases ninefold.
Speed halves, wavelength halves, intensity triples.

explanation:
- Sound speed remains approximately constant in the same air.
- Since v=flambda, doubling frequency halves wavelength.
- Intensity is proportional to amplitude squared, so tripling amplitude increases intensity by 3²=9.

title: Echoes and the Persistence of Hearing
question: A student stands 18 m from a large wall. A short sound pulse is reflected back to the student. Take the speed of sound as 330 m/s. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The round-trip time is approximately 0.109 s, so a distinct echo is possible under ordinary conditions.
The round-trip time is approximately 0.055 s, so a distinct echo is always heard.
The round-trip time is approximately 0.218 s, because the sound travels four times the distance.
The round-trip time is approximately 0.009 s, so the wall cannot reflect sound.

explanation:
t=(2d / v)
=(2(18) / 330)
≈0.109 s


This is slightly greater than the usual 0.1 s persistence-of-hearing threshold. A distinct echo is therefore possible, though real audibility also depends on the reflected sound's strength and the surroundings.

title: Closed Pipe Versus Open Pipe
question: An ideal closed pipe and an ideal open pipe have the same effective length and are filled with air under the same conditions. Which comparison of their fundamental frequencies is correct?

options.text: The closed pipe has twice the fundamental frequency of the open pipe.
The open pipe has twice the fundamental frequency of the closed pipe.
Both have identical fundamental frequencies because their lengths are equal.
The closed pipe has four times the fundamental frequency of the open pipe.

explanation:
For equal effective length L,


f_{closed}=(v / 4L),
qquad
f_{open}=(v / 2L)


Hence f_{open}=2f_{closed}.

title: A Closed Pipe's Harmonics
question: An ideal closed pipe has a fundamental frequency of 150 Hz. Which frequency is **not** an allowed resonance frequency in the ideal model?

options.text: 150 Hz
450 Hz
750 Hz
600 Hz

explanation:
The ideal closed pipe supports odd harmonics only:


f_n=f₁,3f₁,5f₁,ldots


The allowed frequencies include 150, 450 and 750 Hz. The frequency 600 Hz=4f₁ is an even harmonic and is not an allowed resonance in this ideal model.

title: Sonometer — Two Variables Change
question: A stretched string initially vibrates at frequency f. Its length is doubled, its tension is quadrupled and its linear density remains unchanged. What is the new fundamental frequency?

options.text: f
2f
4f

explanation:
For a stretched string,


f=(1 / 2L)√((T / µ))


The new frequency ratio is


(f₂ / f₁)
=(L₁ / 2L₁)
√((4T₁ / T₁))
=frac12(2)=1


The two changes exactly cancel, so the frequency remains unchanged.

title: Intensity, Amplitude and Distance
question: A point source emits sound uniformly in all directions. At distance r, the sound has intensity I and amplitude A. At distance 3r, neglecting absorption, what are the intensity and amplitude?

options.text: I/3 and A/3
I/9 and A/9
I/9 and A/3
I/3 and A/9

explanation: Spherical spreading gives Ipropto1/r², so the intensity becomes I/9. Since Ipropto A², the amplitude becomes A/3.

title: Forced Vibrations Versus Resonance
question: A tuning fork of frequency 256 Hz is held near a second fork of natural frequency 320 Hz. The second fork begins vibrating weakly. Which statement is most accurate?

options.text: The second fork undergoes forced vibrations, but strong resonance is not expected because the natural and driving frequencies differ.
The second fork cannot vibrate because its natural frequency differs from the first fork's frequency.
The second fork must vibrate strongly because any forced vibration is resonance.
The second fork immediately changes its natural frequency to 256 Hz.

explanation: A periodic sound disturbance can force the second fork to vibrate even when the frequencies differ. The response is generally strongest near resonance, when the driving frequency matches the natural frequency.

title: Air Column and Frequency Change
question: A closed resonance tube is initially resonant with a tuning fork at its first resonance. The tuning fork is replaced with one of higher frequency, while the speed of sound remains unchanged. What happens to the physical air-column length required for the first resonance, ignoring end-correction changes?

options.text: It increases in direct proportion to frequency.
It remains unchanged because the tube is the same.
It doubles for every doubling of frequency.
It decreases because the wavelength is shorter.

explanation:
For first resonance in a closed pipe,


L_{eff}=(lambda / 4)
=(v / 4f)


A higher frequency gives a shorter wavelength and therefore a shorter first-resonance air column.

title: Speed of Sound — Temperature Versus Frequency
question: A source emits sound at 400 Hz in air. The air temperature rises while the source frequency remains unchanged. Which combination is correct?

options.text: Speed decreases and wavelength increases.
Speed increases and wavelength increases.
Speed increases and wavelength decreases.
Speed and wavelength both remain unchanged.

explanation: Sound speed increases as air becomes warmer. With frequency fixed, v=flambda, so wavelength must increase in the same proportion as speed.

title: Hearing Range and Ultrasound
question: A device produces sound at 25 kHz and another produces sound at 18 kHz. Under the usual approximate human hearing limits, which statement is correct?

options.text: Both are ultrasonic because both are above 10 kHz.
Both are audible because all sound below 30 kHz is audible.
The 25 kHz sound is ultrasonic, while the 18 kHz sound lies within the usual audible range.
The 18 kHz sound is infrasonic, while the 25 kHz sound is audible.

explanation: The usual upper limit of human hearing is approximately 20 kHz. Thus, 25 kHz is ultrasonic, while 18 kHz is within the usual audible range, although actual hearing limits vary among individuals.

title: Two Cliffs — Multiple Echoes
question: A person stands between two cliffs. The person is 330 m from the nearer cliff and 660 m from the farther cliff. The speed of sound is 330 m/s. Which pair gives the round-trip times for the first echoes from the nearer and farther cliffs?

options.text: 1 s and 2 s
2 s and 4 s
1 s and 4 s
0.5 s and 1 s

explanation:
For an echo, the sound travels to the cliff and back:


t_{near}=(2(330) / 330)=2 s



t_{far}=(2(660) / 330)=4 s

title: Sound Intensity and Decibel Difference
question: Two sounds have intensities in the ratio 100:1. Using the intensity-level relation Δβ=10log_≤ft((I₁ / I₂)right), what is their sound-level difference?

options.text: 10 dB
100 dB
2 dB
20 dB

explanation:
Δβ=10log_{10}(100)
=10(2)=20 dB


A hundredfold increase in intensity corresponds to a 20 dB increase, not a hundredfold increase in the decibel value.
