options.text: The instrument with stronger higher harmonics must have a lower fundamental frequency.
The instruments must sound identical because their fundamental frequencies are equal.
Their pitches may be the same, but their qualities or timbres can differ.
The instrument with stronger higher harmonics necessarily produces sound that travels faster.

explanation: The fundamental frequency largely determines pitch. The relative strengths of harmonics influence waveform and timbre, allowing two instruments to sound different while playing the same note.

title: Resonance and Damping — Integrated Concept
question: Two systems have the same natural frequency but different damping. Both are driven at that frequency with the same periodic force. Which statement is generally correct?

options.text: The less-damped system generally develops a larger resonant amplitude.
The more-damped system must develop a larger resonant amplitude because it loses more energy.
Both systems must have identical amplitudes because their natural frequencies are equal.
Neither system can resonate unless damping is exactly zero.

explanation: Damping dissipates energy and limits the amplitude. For comparable systems driven near resonance, the less-damped system generally has a larger resonant response. Resonance does not require damping to be exactly zero.

title: Reflection and Sound Energy
question: A sound pulse strikes a large, hard, smooth wall. Which statement best distinguishes reflection from absorption?

options.text: Reflection converts sound into light, whereas absorption converts sound into electrical energy.
Reflection redirects some sound energy, while absorption transfers some incident sound energy into other forms, commonly internal energy.
Reflection occurs only when all incident energy is absorbed.
Absorption always increases the reflected sound's frequency.

explanation: Reflection redirects sound energy from a boundary. Absorption removes part of the sound energy from the reflected wave, often converting it into thermal energy. Real surfaces can both reflect and absorb sound.

title: Comparing Frequencies and Wavelengths Across Media
question: A sound of frequency 500 Hz travels from air into water. Which statement is correct at the boundary, assuming the source frequency remains fixed?

options.text: Its frequency increases because sound travels faster in water.
Its frequency decreases because the wavelength increases.
Both frequency and wavelength remain unchanged because the source is unchanged.
Its frequency remains 500 Hz, while its wavelength changes because the propagation speed changes.

explanation: The source fixes the frequency, so it remains 500 Hz across the boundary. Since sound generally travels faster in water than in air, its wavelength in water is correspondingly greater.

title: Comparing Two Strings — Linear Density Trap
question: Two stretched strings have the same length and tension. String X has linear density µ, while string Y has linear density 4µ. What is the ratio of their fundamental frequencies, f_X:f_Y?
explanation:
For equal length and tension,


fproptofrac1{√(µ)}


Thus,


f_X:f_Y
=frac1{√(µ)}:frac1{√(4µ)}
=1:frac12=2:1


The heavier string has half the fundamental frequency.

title: Echo Measurement — Hidden Round-Trip Error
question: A student stands 49.5 m from a wall and hears an echo 0.30 s after producing a sharp sound. The student calculates the speed of sound by dividing the wall distance by the echo time. What is the correct speed, assuming negligible delay in sound production and detection?
explanation:
The sound travels to the wall and back, so the total distance is 2(49.5)=99 m.


v=(99 / 0.30)=330 m/s


The common error is using only the one-way distance.

title: Sound Boards in Auditoriums
question: A sound board is placed behind a speaker on a stage. Which statement best explains its intended function?

options.text: It reflects sound towards the audience, helping direct sound energy into the desired region.
It increases the speed of sound by compressing the air permanently.
It changes longitudinal sound waves into transverse waves.
It eliminates all reflections from the auditorium, including unwanted echoes.

explanation: A sound board is designed to reflect and direct sound towards listeners. It does not change the wave type or eliminate every reflection in the room.

title: Grand-Master Integrated Question
question: A tuning fork produces sound in air at 330 m/s. Its frequency is increased from 440 Hz to 660 Hz, and its vibration amplitude is doubled. Assume the same medium and comparable conditions. Which complete set of conclusions is correct?

options.text: The wavelength increases from 0.75 m to 1.00 m, and the intensity doubles.
The wavelength decreases from 0.75 m to 0.50 m, and the intensity doubles.
The wavelength remains 0.75 m, and the intensity becomes four times as great because the frequency changed.
The wavelength decreases from 0.75 m to 0.50 m, and the intensity becomes four times as great.

explanation:
Initially,


lambda₁=(330 / 440)=0.75 m


After increasing frequency,


lambda₂=(330 / 660)=0.50 m


Doubling amplitude multiplies intensity by 2²=4. The frequency change alters wavelength, while the amplitude change alters intensity.

title: Nature of Sound — Assertion–Reason
question: Assertion (A):** Sound cannot propagate through a perfect vacuum. **Reason (R):** Sound propagation requires particles of a medium to transfer mechanical disturbances from one region to another.

options.text: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A.
Both A and R are true, but R does not correctly explain A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

explanation:
Assertion (A):** Sound cannot propagate through a perfect vacuum.

**Reason (R):** Sound propagation requires particles of a medium to transfer mechanical disturbances from one region to another.

A) Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A.
B) Both A and R are true, but R does not correctly explain A.
C) A is true, but R is false.
D) A is false, but R is true.

**Correct Answer: A**

**Reason:** Sound is a mechanical wave. In a vacuum, there are no particles to transmit the disturbance. The absence of a material medium prevents sound propagation.

title: Longitudinal Waves — Incorrect Statement
question: Which statement about a sound wave travelling through air is **incorrect**?

options.text: Air particles oscillate approximately parallel to the direction of wave propagation.
Compressions correspond to regions of relatively high pressure.
Rarefactions correspond to regions where air particles cease vibrating momentarily and remain permanently separated.
The disturbance travels through the medium while individual particles oscillate about their equilibrium positions.

explanation: Rarefactions are regions of lower pressure and density, not regions where particles stop vibrating permanently. The particles continue oscillating about their equilibrium positions.

title: Frequency and Time Period — Conceptual Trap
question: A tuning fork is replaced by another fork whose frequency is twice as great. Both produce sound waves travelling through the same air at the same temperature. Which change occurs?

options.text: The wavelength doubles and the time period halves.
The wavelength halves and the time period halves.
The wavelength remains unchanged and the time period halves.
The wavelength halves and the time period remains unchanged.

explanation: In the same medium under unchanged conditions, the speed remains approximately constant. Since v=flambda, doubling f halves lambda. Also, T=1/f, so the time period halves.

title: Propagation Speed — Assertion–Reason
question: Assertion (A):** Two sound waves of different frequencies can travel through the same air at the same speed. **Reason (R):** In a given medium under the same physical conditions, sound speed is determined primarily by the medium's properties, not by the frequency of the sound.

options.text: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A.
Both A and R are true, but R does not correctly explain A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

explanation:
Assertion (A):** Two sound waves of different frequencies can travel through the same air at the same speed.

**Reason (R):** In a given medium under the same physical conditions, sound speed is determined primarily by the medium's properties, not by the frequency of the sound.

A) Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A.
B) Both A and R are true, but R does not correctly explain A.
C) A is true, but R is false.
D) A is false, but R is true.

**Correct Answer: A**

**Reason:** In ordinary school-level treatment, sound speed in a given medium remains independent of frequency. Different frequencies therefore correspond to different wavelengths when the speed is the same.

title: Sound Speed in Different Media
question: Sound travels through air, water and steel under suitable conditions. Which statement is generally correct?

options.text: Sound travels fastest in air because its particles move freely.
Sound travels at the same speed in all three because the source determines the speed.
Sound travels fastest in water because liquids are denser than gases.
Sound generally travels fastest in steel, slower in water and slower still in air.

explanation: Sound speed depends on both the medium's elasticity and density. In general, solids transmit sound faster than liquids, which transmit it faster than gases. Density alone does not determine sound speed.

title: Temperature and Sound Speed
question: The temperature of a sample of air increases while its composition and pressure remain approximately unchanged. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Sound speed increases, and at a fixed frequency its wavelength increases.
Sound speed decreases, and at a fixed frequency its wavelength decreases.
Sound speed increases, but its wavelength must remain unchanged.
Sound speed remains constant because pressure is unchanged.

explanation: Sound travels faster in warmer air. For a fixed source frequency, v=flambda; therefore, an increase in speed produces an increase in wavelength.

title: Pressure and Frequency — Distinguishing Dependencies
question: Consider the following statements about sound travelling through air. 1. Increasing the frequency of the source necessarily increases the sound speed in the same air under unchanged conditions. 2. Increasing the pressure while keeping the temperature constant necessarily increases the sound speed in an ideal gas. 3. Increasing the source frequency in the same medium decreases the wavelength if the speed remains unchanged. Which statements are correct?

options.text: 1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
3 only
1 and 3 only

explanation: In the ideal-gas model, sound speed depends on temperature and the gas properties; it does not necessarily increase merely because pressure increases at constant temperature. Frequency does not determine the speed in the same medium, but v=flambda means wavelength decreases when frequency increases at constant speed.

title: Reflection of Sound — Law of Reflection
question: A sound ray strikes a smooth reflecting surface obliquely. Which statement correctly describes ideal specular reflection?

options.text: The angle of reflection is measured from the reflecting surface and equals the angle of incidence measured from the normal.
The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, both measured from the normal to the surface.
The angle of reflection is always twice the angle of incidence.
Sound obeys the law of reflection only when the reflecting surface is perfectly rigid.

explanation: The angles of incidence and reflection are measured from the normal and are equal. The law is not expressed by measuring one angle from the surface and the other from the normal.

title: Persistence of Hearing — Echo Condition
question: A distinct echo is heard only when the reflected sound reaches the listener sufficiently late after the original sound. Which explanation is most appropriate?

options.text: The reflected sound must have a higher frequency than the original sound.
The reflecting surface must absorb all frequencies except the fundamental.
The original sound must have a longer wavelength than the reflected sound.
The time gap must be about 0.1 s or more for the ear to distinguish the echo under ordinary conditions.

explanation:
is most appropriate?

A) The reflected sound must have a higher frequency than the original sound.
B) The reflecting surface must absorb all frequencies except the fundamental.
C) The original sound must have a longer wavelength than the reflected sound.
D) The time gap must be about 0.1 s or more for the ear to distinguish the echo under ordinary conditions.

**Correct Answer: D**

**Reason:** Persistence of hearing is approximately 0.1 s. If the reflected sound arrives too soon, it merges perceptually with the original sound instead of being heard as a separate echo.

title: Echo Versus Reverberation
question: Which situation most clearly demonstrates **reverberation rather than a distinct echo**?

options.text: A single reflected sound is heard distinctly after a sufficiently long delay.
A sonar pulse returns from a distant seabed after a measurable interval.
Reflected sounds overlap with the original sound and with one another, prolonging the sound in a hall.
A shout is heard again after reflection from a distant cliff.

explanation: Reverberation occurs when numerous reflections arrive close enough together to prolong the audible sound. A distinct echo is heard as a separate repetition.

title: Controlling Reverberation
question: A lecture hall produces excessive reverberation. Which modification would most directly reduce it?

options.text: Covering suitable wall and ceiling areas with sound-absorbing materials.
Replacing all absorbing surfaces with smooth polished metal.
Increasing the reflecting area of the walls without adding absorption.
Increasing the loudspeaker frequency while keeping the hall unchanged.

explanation: Porous acoustic materials, curtains and upholstered surfaces absorb part of the incident sound energy, reducing repeated reflections. Smooth hard surfaces generally reflect more sound.

title: Megaphones and Sound Boards
question: A megaphone helps direct sound towards an audience mainly because it:

options.text: increases the frequency of the speaker's voice.
channels sound preferentially in a desired direction through its shape.
converts longitudinal sound waves into transverse waves.
increases the speed of sound in the surrounding air.

explanation: The shape of a megaphone helps direct sound forward and reduces its spreading in unwanted directions. It does not change the nature of the wave or the speed of sound in air.

title: Stethoscope — Physical Principle
question: A stethoscope helps a doctor hear internal body sounds more clearly. Which explanation is the most appropriate at this level?

options.text: It converts sound directly into light and then back into sound.
It eliminates the need for mechanical vibrations in the earpieces.
It increases the frequency of every sound entering the chest piece.
It conveys body-generated sounds through its structure to the listener's ears, helping make weak sounds audible.

explanation:
is the most appropriate at this level?

A) It converts sound directly into light and then back into sound.
B) It eliminates the need for mechanical vibrations in the earpieces.
C) It increases the frequency of every sound entering the chest piece.
D) It conveys body-generated sounds through its structure to the listener's ears, helping make weak sounds audible.

**Correct Answer: D**

**Reason:** The stethoscope provides a pathway for transmitting body sounds to the ears. Its operation does not require increasing the frequency of the original sound.

title: Natural and Forced Vibrations
question: A tuning fork is struck and then allowed to vibrate freely in air. A nearby second tuning fork begins vibrating weakly when the first fork sounds. Which statement correctly distinguishes the two forks' motions?

options.text: Both forks must be vibrating only at the frequency of the room's air molecules.
The struck fork undergoes forced vibrations, while the second undergoes natural vibrations without an external cause.
The struck fork initially vibrates freely at its natural frequency, while the second undergoes forced vibrations due to the periodic sound disturbance.
The second fork can vibrate only if it has a higher natural frequency than the first fork.

explanation: The struck fork vibrates freely at its natural frequency after being excited. The second fork receives a periodic driving disturbance from the sound and undergoes forced vibrations.

title: Resonance — Necessary Condition
question: Which statement most accurately describes resonance in a simple vibrating system?

options.text: Resonance occurs whenever the applied force has a greater amplitude than the restoring force.
Resonance occurs when the driving frequency matches the natural frequency, producing a particularly large response under suitable conditions.
Resonance requires the driving frequency to be exactly twice the natural frequency.
Resonance is possible only in systems that vibrate without any energy loss.

explanation: Resonance occurs when the driving frequency matches the natural frequency. Damping limits the amplitude, so a completely lossless system is not a necessary condition for resonance.

title: Damped Vibrations — Energy Consideration
question: A vibrating tuning fork produces progressively weaker sound as time passes. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Its frequency must continuously fall to zero as its amplitude decreases.
Its amplitude increases because energy is transferred from the surrounding air.
Its natural frequency becomes equal to the frequency of every sound nearby.
Its mechanical energy is gradually dissipated, while its frequency may remain approximately constant.

explanation: Damping removes mechanical energy, reducing amplitude with time. The frequency need not decrease continuously; for light damping, it remains close to the natural frequency.

title: Resonance Tube — Successive Resonances
question: In a resonance-tube experiment using a tuning fork of fixed frequency, two successive resonance positions are observed. Which statement is correct under ideal conditions?

options.text: Their air-column lengths differ by approximately half a wavelength.
Their air-column lengths differ by one full wavelength.
The first resonance must occur at an air-column length equal to one full wavelength.
The second resonance occurs at a shorter air-column length than the first.

explanation: For a closed air column, successive resonances occur at lengths differing by lambda/2. The closed end is a displacement node and the open end is approximately a displacement antinode.

title: Closed Organ Pipes — Allowed Frequencies
question: An ideal pipe is closed at one end and open at the other. Which statement about its resonant frequencies is correct?

options.text: Every integer harmonic is present with equal amplitude.
Only even harmonics can occur.
Only odd harmonics occur in the ideal model, with frequencies f,3f,5f,ldots.
The fundamental frequency is twice that of an open pipe of the same effective length.

explanation: A closed pipe supports a displacement node at its closed end and an antinode at its open end. The allowed ideal lengths correspond to odd multiples of a quarter wavelength, giving odd harmonics only.

title: Open Organ Pipes — Harmonic Structure
question: For an ideal open pipe of effective length L, which statement is correct?

options.text: Its fundamental frequency is v/(4L), and only odd harmonics occur.
Its fundamental frequency is v/(2L), and all integer harmonics can occur.
Its fundamental frequency is v/L, and only even harmonics occur.
Its fundamental frequency is 2v/L, and all integer harmonics can occur.

explanation: An open pipe has displacement antinodes at both ends. For the fundamental, L=lambda/2, so f₁=v/(2L). Higher modes occur at integer multiples of the fundamental frequency.

title: Resonance Tube and End Correction
question: Why is the effective length of a resonating air column at an open end slightly greater than its physical length?

options.text: Air particles at the open end form a permanent compression.
The tuning fork increases the physical length of the tube through heating.
The sound wavelength becomes shorter only inside the tube.
The displacement antinode lies slightly beyond the physical open end.

explanation: Air just outside the tube also participates in the vibration. Consequently, the effective air-column length is greater than the measured physical length; this difference is called end correction.

title: Sonometer — Tension and Frequency
question: A sonometer wire is adjusted to resonate with a tuning fork. Without changing the wire's vibrating length or linear mass density, its tension is increased. What happens to its natural frequency?

options.text: It increases because the wave speed on the wire increases.
It decreases because the wire becomes harder to displace.
It remains unchanged because the tuning fork determines the wire's natural frequency.
It becomes zero unless the vibrating length is also increased.

explanation: For a stretched string, f=(1 / 2L)√((T / µ)). At fixed length and linear density, increasing tension increases the wave speed and natural frequency.

title: Sonometer — Resonance Versus Loudness
question: A sonometer wire vibrates with maximum amplitude when correctly adjusted to resonate with a tuning fork. Which statement best explains the observation?

options.text: The tuning fork transfers energy only when the wire's tension is zero.
Resonance forces the wire to vibrate at a frequency unrelated to its own natural frequency.
The driving frequency matches the wire's natural frequency, allowing efficient energy transfer.
The wire's amplitude becomes large because its linear density increases automatically.

explanation: When the driving frequency matches the natural frequency, energy transfer is especially effective. The resulting large amplitude makes the wire's vibration more noticeable.

title: Loudness, Intensity and Amplitude
question: Two sound waves of the same frequency travel through the same medium. Under comparable conditions, the amplitude of one wave is doubled. Which statement is correct in the usual school-level model?

options.text: Its frequency doubles and its pitch rises by one octave.
Its intensity becomes four times as great, although perceived loudness need not become exactly four times as great.
Its wavelength doubles and its intensity becomes twice as great.
Its speed doubles because its amplitude has increased.

explanation: For sound waves under comparable conditions, intensity is proportional to the square of amplitude. Doubling amplitude therefore gives four times the intensity. Perceived loudness is not simply proportional to intensity.

title: Pitch Versus Quality
question: Two musical instruments produce the same note at the same fundamental frequency and comparable loudness, yet their sounds remain distinguishable. The principal reason is that they may differ in:

options.text: the speed of sound in the surrounding air.
the time required for sound to travel one metre through air.
the pitch, which must be different whenever two instruments sound different.
the waveform and relative strengths of their overtones, giving them different qualities or timbres.

explanation:
is that they may differ in:

A) the speed of sound in the surrounding air.
B) the time required for sound to travel one metre through air.
C) the pitch, which must be different whenever two instruments sound different.
D) the waveform and relative strengths of their overtones, giving them different qualities or timbres.

**Correct Answer: D**

**Reason:** Pitch is associated primarily with frequency, whereas quality or timbre allows sounds of similar pitch and loudness to be distinguished. Their harmonic content and waveform may differ.

title: Audible, Infrasonic and Ultrasonic Sounds
question: Consider the following statements. 1. Infrasonic sound has a frequency below the usual lower limit of human hearing. 2. Ultrasonic sound has a frequency above the usual upper limit of human hearing. 3. Ultrasound is necessarily more intense than every audible sound. 4. A sound's classification as ultrasonic depends on its frequency, not on whether it is loud or faint. Which option is correct?

options.text: 1, 2 and 4 only
1 and 3 only
2, 3 and 4 only

explanation: The usual human audible range is approximately 20 Hz to 20{,}000 Hz. Frequency determines whether a sound is infrasonic, audible or ultrasonic. Ultrasound need not be more intense than audible sound.

title: Uses of Ultrasound
question: Which pairing is **incorrect**?

options.text: Medical ultrasonography — forming images using reflected ultrasonic waves.
SONAR — using reflected sound pulses to determine underwater distance or depth.
Detecting internal cracks in metal — using the transmission and reflection of ultrasonic waves.
Measuring the colour of a distant object directly — using the time taken by an ultrasonic echo.

explanation: Ultrasonic echoes can provide information about distance and internal structure, but echo time does not directly measure colour. SONAR, medical imaging and flaw detection are established applications.

title: Sound Versus Light — Fundamental Difference
question: A loud explosion occurs far from an observer. The observer sees the flash before hearing the explosion. Which explanation is correct?

options.text: Light must always be produced before sound by the source.
Light travels much faster than sound in air, so the flash reaches the observer first.
Sound cannot travel through air over large distances.
The sound wave must have a lower frequency than the light wave, so it travels more slowly.

explanation:
is correct?

A) Light must always be produced before sound by the source.
B) Light travels much faster than sound in air, so the flash reaches the observer first.
C) Sound cannot travel through air over large distances.
D) The sound wave must have a lower frequency than the light wave, so it travels more slowly.

**Correct Answer: B**

**Reason:** Light travels vastly faster than sound in air. The delay is primarily due to their different propagation speeds, not a requirement that sound have a lower frequency.

title: Humidity and Sound Speed
question: Under ordinary atmospheric conditions, increasing the humidity of air at approximately the same temperature generally causes the speed of sound to:

options.text: decrease because water vapour always makes air denser.
remain exactly unchanged under all atmospheric conditions.
increase because humid air is generally less dense than dry air at the same temperature and pressure.
become independent of temperature.

explanation: At the same temperature and pressure, humid air is generally less dense than dry air because water vapour has a lower molar mass than the average dry-air mixture. Sound speed therefore generally increases slightly.

title: Sound Intensity Versus Distance
question: A small sound source radiates approximately uniformly in all directions. If the observer moves from distance r to distance 2r, with negligible absorption and reflections, which statement is correct?

options.text: Intensity becomes half, and amplitude becomes half.
Intensity becomes one-quarter, and amplitude becomes one-quarter.
Intensity remains constant, while frequency becomes half.
Intensity becomes one-quarter, while amplitude becomes approximately half.

explanation: For approximately spherical spreading, intensity varies as 1/r². Doubling distance reduces intensity to one-quarter. Since intensity is proportional to amplitude squared under comparable conditions, amplitude becomes approximately half.

title: Comprehensive Conceptual Trap — Sound-Wave Properties
question: A source produces a sound wave in air. The source is then changed so that the new sound has a higher frequency and greater amplitude, while the air conditions remain unchanged. Which conclusion is correct?

options.text: The new sound has a shorter wavelength and greater intensity, while its speed in air remains approximately unchanged.
The new sound has a greater wavelength and greater speed because both frequency and amplitude increased.
The new sound has a shorter wavelength but lower intensity because its frequency increased.
The new sound has unchanged wavelength and speed, but its time period increases.

explanation: In the same air under unchanged conditions, sound speed remains approximately constant. Increasing frequency therefore decreases wavelength, while increasing amplitude increases intensity. The two changes affect different wave properties.

title: A listener moving away from a reflecting wall
question: A person stands 49.5 m from a wall and produces a short sound. Immediately afterwards, the person moves directly away from the wall at 10 m s^. The speed of sound is 330 m s^. How long after emission does the echo reach the person?
explanation:
The sound reaches the stationary wall in


t₁=(49.5 / 330)=0.15 s.


During this time, the person moves 10(0.15)=1.5 m away from the wall.

The return distance is 49.5+1.5=51 m. Since the person moves away from the returning sound, the separation closes at 330-10=320 m s^{-1}.


t₂=(51 / 320)=0.159375 s.


Total time:


t=0.15+0.159375=0.309375 s.


The correct answer is approximately **0.309 s**, which is absent from the options. The options must be corrected; option A is the stationary-listener result.

title: Finding frequency from a wave train
question: A source produces 1500 complete vibrations in 3.75 s. The resulting sound travels through air at 330 m s^. What is the wavelength?
explanation:
f=(1500 / 3.75)=400 Hz


Then


lambda=(v / f)=(330 / 400)=0.825 m.


The correct answer is **A**, not C. Option C results from using an incorrect frequency.

title: Successive resonances in a closed tube
question: A resonance tube gives successive resonance lengths of 21.5 cm and 55.5 cm. The speed of sound is 340 m s^. What is the frequency of the sound?

options.text: 250 Hz
500 Hz
125 Hz

explanation:
Successive resonances differ by half a wavelength:


(lambda / 2)=55.5-21.5=34.0 cm.


Thus,


lambda=0.68 m.


Therefore,


f=(340 / 0.68)=500 Hz.


Option A is half the correct frequency because it incorrectly treats the difference between successive resonances as a full wavelength.

title: Fundamental frequency of a closed pipe with end correction
question: A closed pipe has a physical length of 42 cm and an end correction of 1.5 cm. The speed of sound is 330 m s^. Find the fundamental frequency.

options.text: 375 Hz

explanation:
The effective length is


L_{eff}=42+1.5=43.5 cm=0.435 m.


For the fundamental of a closed pipe,


f₁=(v / 4L_{eff)}
=(330 / 4(0.435))
≈189.7 Hz.


The correct result is approximately **189.7 Hz**, absent from the options. The option values need correction.

title: Comparing two strings with different tensions and densities
question: String P has length L, tension T and linear density µ. String Q has length L/2, tension T/2 and linear density 2µ. Both vibrate in their fundamental modes. If P has a fundamental frequency of 300 Hz, what is the fundamental frequency of Q?

options.text: 150 Hz
300 Hz
600 Hz
75 Hz

explanation:
Using


f=(1 / 2L)√((T / µ)),


the ratio is


(f_Q / f_P)
=(L / L/2)
√(((T/2)/(2µ) / T/µ))
=2√(frac14)=1.


Thus f_Q=300 Hz. Option C incorrectly accounts for the halved length but ignores the reduced tension and increased linear density.

title: Comparing the loudness of two sounds
question: Under identical conditions, sound P has an amplitude of 2 mm, while sound Q has an amplitude of 5 mm. If the intensity of P is 4 W m^, what is the intensity of Q?
explanation:
Intensity is proportional to the square of amplitude:


(I_Q / I_P)=≤ft(frac52right)²=6.25.


Therefore,


I_Q=4(6.25)=25 W m^{-2}.


Option A incorrectly assumes that intensity is directly proportional to amplitude.

title: Echo from a wall when the air temperature changes
question: A person stands 66 m from a wall. At one temperature, sound travels at 330 m s^; at a higher temperature, its speed becomes 350 m s^. Assuming the wall and person remain stationary, how much does the echo-return time decrease?
explanation:
Initially,


t₁=(2(66) / 330)=0.400 s.


At the higher temperature,


t₂=(132 / 350)≈0.37714 s.


The decrease is


Δ t=0.400-0.37714≈0.02286 s.


Hence the answer is approximately 0.0229 s, option C.

title: Fundamental frequency of an open pipe
question: An open organ pipe has a length of 1.10 m. If the speed of sound is 330 m s^, what is its fundamental frequency, neglecting end correction?

options.text: 75 Hz
150 Hz
330 Hz
300 Hz

explanation:
For an open pipe,


f₁=(v / 2L)
=(330 / 2.20)=150 Hz.


Option C confuses the speed of sound with the frequency.

title: A closed pipe and its fifth harmonic
question: A closed pipe has an effective length of 0.60 m. If the speed of sound is 360 m s^, what is the frequency of its fifth harmonic?

options.text: 150 Hz
300 Hz
450 Hz
750 Hz

explanation:
For a closed pipe, the fifth harmonic is


f₅=(5v / 4L)
=(5(360) / 4(0.60))
=(1800 / 2.4)=750 Hz.


Option C corresponds to the third harmonic.

title: Calculating the time period from a harmonic frequency
question: A stretched string produces its sixth harmonic at 1440 Hz. What is the time period of its fundamental vibration?
explanation:
The fundamental frequency is


f₁=(1440 / 6)=240 Hz.


Hence,


T₁=frac1{240}=4.17×10^{-3} s.


Option B gives the period of the sixth harmonic, not the fundamental.

title: Distance from a wall using a distinct echo
question: A person hears an echo 0.24 s after producing a sound. The speed of sound is 330 m s^. How far away is the reflecting wall?
explanation:
The total distance travelled by the sound is


d_{total}=330(0.24)=79.2 m.


The wall is half that distance away:


d=(79.2 / 2)=39.6 m.


Option A gives the round-trip distance.

title: Finding the new frequency when a string's length changes
question: A string vibrates at 480 Hz in its fundamental mode. Its length is increased by 25%, while tension and linear density remain unchanged. What is the new fundamental frequency?

options.text: 384 Hz
600 Hz
240 Hz
400 Hz

explanation:
For constant tension and linear density,


fproptofrac1L.


The new length is 1.25L, so


f₂=(480 / 1.25)=384 Hz.


Option B incorrectly increases the frequency when the string becomes longer.

title: Two sound pulses travelling in opposite directions
question: Two sound pulses are emitted simultaneously from opposite ends of a straight tunnel of length 990 m. Both travel through air at 330 m s^. After how long do they meet?
explanation:
The closing speed is 330+330=660 m s^{-1}.


t=(990 / 660)=1.5 s.


Option B calculates the time taken by one pulse to travel the entire tunnel.

title: Finding the speed of sound from wavelength and period
question: A sound wave has a time period of 2.0×10^ s and a wavelength of 0.66 m. Calculate its speed.
explanation:
f=frac1T=frac1{0.002}=500 Hz.


Then


v=flambda=500(0.66)=330 m s^{-1}.


The correct answer is **B**, not C. Option C doubles the correct speed.

title: String frequency when both tension and linear density change
question: A string vibrates at 300 Hz. Its tension is increased to nine times the original tension, and its linear density becomes four times the original value. Its length is unchanged. What is the new frequency?

options.text: 450 Hz
600 Hz
900 Hz

explanation:
fpropto√((T / µ)).


Therefore,


(f₂ / f₁)=√((9 / 4))=frac32.


So,


f₂=300≤ft(frac32right)=450 Hz.


Option C considers the tension change but ignores the increased linear density.

title: Finding the frequency of a closed pipe's fundamental mode
question: A closed pipe has a physical length of 0.80 m and an end correction of 0.02 m. If the speed of sound is 330 m s^, calculate the fundamental frequency.

options.text: 100 Hz

explanation:
The effective length is


L_{eff}=0.80+0.02=0.82 m.


For the fundamental of a closed pipe,


f₁=(330 / 4(0.82))
≈100.61 Hz.


The correct result is approximately **100.6 Hz**, which is not listed exactly. Option D is the closest but is not exact; the options should be corrected.

title: Calculating the depth of a reflecting surface underwater
question: A sonar system sends an ultrasonic pulse through water at 1480 m s^. The echo returns after 1.8 s. What is the depth of the reflecting surface?
explanation:
The total distance travelled is


d_{total}=1480(1.8)=2664 m.


The depth is half the round-trip distance:


d=(2664 / 2)=1332 m.


Option A gives the total pulse path rather than the depth.

title: Comparing two frequencies in the same medium
question: A sound wave of frequency 250 Hz has a wavelength of 1.32 m. Another sound wave travels in the same medium with a frequency of 550 Hz. What is its wavelength?
explanation:
The speed in the medium is


v=250(1.32)=330 m s^{-1}.


For the second wave,


lambda₂=(330 / 550)=0.60 m.


Option B incorrectly assumes wavelength increases with frequency in a fixed medium.

title: Calculating the frequency from successive resonance lengths
question: A resonance tube gives successive resonance lengths of 24 cm and 64 cm. The speed of sound is 320 m s^. What is the frequency?

options.text: 200 Hz
400 Hz
800 Hz
160 Hz

explanation:
(lambda / 2)=64-24=40 cm.


Thus lambda=0.80 m.


f=(320 / 0.80)=400 Hz.


The correct answer is **B**, not A. Option A is half the actual frequency.

title: Frequency ratio of two strings
question: Two strings have the same length and the same linear density. String P has tension T, while string Q has tension 9T. If P vibrates at 160 Hz, what is the fundamental frequency of Q?

options.text: 480 Hz
320 Hz

explanation:
For strings of equal length and linear density,


fproptosqrt T.


Therefore,


f_Q=160sqrt9=160(3)=480 Hz.


Option B incorrectly assumes frequency is directly proportional to tension.

title: Comparing sound travel times through two media
question: A sound pulse travels through a 660 m steel rail at 5280 m s^. A second pulse travels through 660 m of air at 330 m s^. What is the difference between the two travel times?
explanation:
Travel time through steel:


t_s=(660 / 5280)=0.125 s.


Travel time through air:


t_a=(660 / 330)=2.00 s.


Difference:


Δ t=2.00-0.125=1.875 s.


The correct answer is **A**, not B. Option B results from subtracting incorrectly.

title: Determining the fundamental frequency of a string from its harmonics
question: A stretched string vibrates in its fourth harmonic at 880 Hz. Its tension, vibrating length and linear density remain unchanged. What is the frequency of its sixth harmonic?

options.text: 220 Hz

explanation:
For a stretched string, the harmonic frequencies are integer multiples of the fundamental frequency.


f₄=4f₁=880 Hz


Therefore,


f₁=(880 / 4)=220 Hz.


The sixth harmonic is


f₆=6(220)=1320 Hz.


Option A corresponds to the fifth harmonic, not the sixth.

title: Wave speed, frequency and wavelength
question: A sound wave travels through a medium at 330 m s^. A detector measures 825 complete oscillations in 2.5 seconds. What is the distance between two successive compressions?
explanation:
First calculate frequency:


f=(825 / 2.5)=330 Hz


The distance between successive compressions is one wavelength:


lambda=(v / f)=(330 / 330)=1.00 m


The correct result is **1.00 m**, so option A is correct. Option B incorrectly treats the number of oscillations per second as the wavelength calculation.

title: Frequency and time period after a source changes its vibration rate
question: A sound source initially produces 500 oscillations in 2 seconds. Its vibration rate is then increased by 20%, while the medium remains unchanged. What is the new time period?
explanation:
Initial frequency:


f₁=(500 / 2)=250 Hz


New frequency:


f₂=250(1.20)=300 Hz


Therefore,


T₂=frac1{300}=3.33×10^{-3} s


The correct answer is **3.33×10^{-3} s**, which is missing from the options. The options must be corrected; the closest-looking distractor is C, but it is not exact.

title: Echo from a wall after a delay
question: A student stands 49.5 m from a wall and emits a short sound. Using 330 m s^ for the speed of sound, how long after emission will the echo return?
explanation:
The sound travels to the wall and back:


d_{total}=2(49.5)=99 m


Hence,


t=(99 / 330)=0.30 s


Option A is the one-way travel time, not the echo-return time.

title: Two echoes from two walls
question: A person stands between two parallel walls. The distances to the nearer and farther walls are 66 m and 99 m, respectively. A short sound is emitted. What is the time interval between the two echoes?
explanation:
The echo times are


t₁=(2(66) / 330)=0.40 s



t₂=(2(99) / 330)=0.60 s


Therefore,


Δ t=0.60-0.40=0.20 s.


Option D gives the farther echo's total return time rather than the interval between echoes.

title: Echo when the listener moves towards the wall
question: A student stands 66 m from a rigid wall and emits a short sound pulse. Immediately afterwards, the student walks towards the wall at 5 m s^. Assume the sound returns along the same straight path and the speed of sound is 330 m s^. How long after emission does the student hear the echo?
explanation:
The sound takes


t₁=(66 / 330)=0.20 s


to reach the wall. During this time, the student moves 5(0.20)=1 m towards the wall.

The returning sound then travels 65 m, while the student moves towards it at 5 m s^{-1}. Their closing speed is 330+5=335 m s^{-1}.


t₂=(65 / 335)≈0.1940 s


Thus,


t=t₁+t₂≈0.3940 s.


The correct answer is approximately **0.394 s**, which is absent from the options. Option A is the stationary-listener result; the options need correction.

title: Determining sound speed from a measured echo
question: An experiment uses a wall at a known distance of 82.5 m. The sound is emitted and its echo is recorded after 0.48 s. What speed of sound does the experiment indicate?
explanation:
The sound covers the round-trip distance:


d=2(82.5)=165 m.


Therefore,


v=(165 / 0.48)=343.75 m s^{-1}.


Option B incorrectly uses half the total distance travelled by sound.

title: Repeated echoes from a distant reflector
question: A student produces a short sound at t=0. The first echo from a distant wall arrives at 0.60 s. The student immediately produces a second identical sound at t=0.80 s. When does the second echo arrive, and what is the interval between the two echoes?

options.text: 1.40 s; interval 0.80 s
1.40 s; interval 0.20 s
1.60 s; interval 1.00 s
1.60 s; interval 0.20 s

explanation:
The second sound is emitted 0.80 s after the first and has the same round-trip time of 0.60 s.


t_{second echo}=0.80+0.60=1.40 s.


The interval between echoes is 1.40-0.60=0.80 s.

The correct result is **1.40 s, with an interval of 0.80 s**. Option A should be marked correct; the current key D is incorrect.

title: Temperature and wavelength
question: A sound source emits a constant frequency of 500 Hz. The speed of sound in air is 330 m s^ at 0°C and 348 m s^ at 30°C. What is the increase in wavelength when the air is warmed?
explanation:
At 0°C,


lambda₁=(330 / 500)=0.660 m.


At 30°C,


lambda₂=(348 / 500)=0.696 m.


Therefore,


Δlambda=0.696-0.660=0.036 m.


The correct answer is **A**, not B. The frequency remains constant because the source is unchanged; the wavelength changes with the speed of sound.

title: Does atmospheric pressure affect sound speed?
question: A sound wave travels through air at 330 m s^ under a specified set of ideal conditions. The pressure is doubled while the temperature and composition remain constant. What is the expected speed of sound under the ideal-gas model?

options.text: 330sqrt2 m s^{-1}

explanation:
For an ideal gas,


v=√((γ P / rho)).


At constant temperature and composition, doubling the pressure also doubles the density. Hence P/rho remains constant, so the speed remains 330 m s^{-1}. Option A incorrectly assumes speed is directly proportional to pressure.

title: Finding the time period from wavelength and speed
question: A sound wave travels at 330 m s^ and has a wavelength of 0.55 m. What is the time period of the vibration?
explanation:
First,


f=(v / lambda)=(330 / 0.55)=600 Hz.


Then,


T=frac1f=frac1{600}=1.67×10^{-3} s.


The correct answer is **B**, not A. Option A is a common decimal-place error.

title: Resonance tube: calculating frequency with end correction
question: A closed resonance tube produces its first resonance at an air-column length of 18 cm. The end correction is 1 cm. If the speed of sound is 330 m s^, what is the frequency of the sound?

options.text: 440 Hz
220 Hz

explanation:
For the first resonance in a closed tube,


L+e=(lambda / 4).


Here L+e=18+1=19 cm=0.19 m.


lambda=4(0.19)=0.76 m.


Therefore,


f=(330 / 0.76)≈434.2 Hz.


The correct answer is approximately **434.2 Hz**, which is not listed. The options must be corrected; option B neglects the end correction.

title: Third harmonic of a closed pipe
question: A pipe closed at one end has an effective length of 0.75 m. The speed of sound is 330 m s^. What is the frequency of its third harmonic?

options.text: 110 Hz
220 Hz
440 Hz
330 Hz

explanation:
For a closed pipe, the third harmonic has


L=(3lambda / 4).


Hence,


lambda=(4L / 3)=frac{4(0.75)}3=1.00 m.


Therefore,


f=(330 / 1.00)=330 Hz.


Option D is correct. The tempting error is to treat the third harmonic of a closed pipe as though it were the third harmonic of an open pipe.

title: Third harmonic of an open pipe
question: An open pipe has a length of 0.90 m. Its third harmonic is produced in air where the speed of sound is 330 m s^. What is the frequency?

options.text: 550 Hz

explanation:
For an open pipe,


f_n=(nv / 2L).


For the third harmonic,


f₃=(3(330) / 2(0.90))
=(990 / 1.8)=550 Hz.


Option A is the fundamental frequency, not the third harmonic.

title: Vibrating string: simultaneous changes in tension and length
question: A sonometer string has a fundamental frequency of 200 Hz. Its vibrating length is reduced to half, while its tension is increased to four times the original value. The linear density remains unchanged. What is the new fundamental frequency?

options.text: 400 Hz
800 Hz
200 Hz
100 Hz

explanation:
For a stretched string,


f=frac1{2L}√(frac Tµ).


Halving the length doubles the frequency. Quadrupling the tension doubles it again.


f₂=200×2×2=800 Hz.


Option A accounts for the length change but ignores the effect of tension.

title: Sonar: calculating sea depth
question: A ship emits an ultrasonic pulse vertically downwards. The reflected pulse returns after 3.2 s. The speed of sound in seawater is 1500 m s^. What is the depth of the sea?
explanation:
The pulse travels down and back, so the total distance is


d_{total}=1500(3.2)=4800 m.


The depth is half the total distance:


d=(4800 / 2)=2400 m.


Option A gives the round-trip distance rather than the depth.

title: String frequency when linear density changes
question: A stretched string vibrates at 240 Hz. Its length and tension remain fixed, but its linear density becomes four times its original value. What is the new fundamental frequency?

options.text: 60 Hz
120 Hz
480 Hz
960 Hz

explanation:
For a stretched string,


fproptofrac1{sqrtµ}


when length and tension remain constant.

Thus,


f₂=(240 / sqrt4)=120 Hz.


Option A incorrectly divides the frequency by four instead of by the square root of four.

title: Wavelength of an ultrasonic wave
question: An ultrasonic transducer emits a sound wave of frequency 40,000 Hz into air. Using 330 m s^ for the speed of sound, calculate its wavelength.
explanation:
lambda=frac vf=(330 / 40,000)
=0.00825 m.


Converting to millimetres,


0.00825×1000=8.25 mm.


Option B is ten times too large because of a conversion error.

title: Number of vibrations in a given time
question: A tuning fork has a frequency of 512 Hz. It is sounded continuously for 1.25 s. How many complete vibrations does it execute during this interval?
explanation:
Frequency is the number of vibrations per second:


N=ft=512(1.25)=640.


Option B gives the number of vibrations in one second, not in 1.25 seconds.

title: Determining the phase relationship between two particles
question: Two particles, P and Q, lie on the same sinusoidal progressive wave. Their separation is 0.75 m, and the wavelength is 1.0 m. The wave travels from left to right. Two particles separated by three-quarters of a wavelength What is the phase difference between P and Q?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 155" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M15 78 H305" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1" /><path d="M15 78 C40 20 65 20 90 78 S140 136 165 78 S215 20 240 78 S290 136 305 78" stroke="#0D9488" stroke-width="2.4" fill="none" /><circle cx="45" cy="43" r="4" fill="#2563eb" /><circle cx="225" cy="43" r="4" fill="#7C3AED" /><path d="M45 43 V78 M225 43 V78" stroke="#64748b" stroke-dasharray="3 3" /><text x="45" y="31" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">P</text><text x="225" y="31" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Q</text><path d="M45 112 H225 M45 108 V116 M225 108 V116" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1" /><text x="135" y="128" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">0.75 m</text><path d="M260 142 H302 M296 137 L303 142 L296 147" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.2" fill="none" /><text x="280" y="135" text-anchor="middle" font-size="9" fill="currentColor">Wave</text></svg>

options.text: 90^°, and they are always moving in the same direction.
180^°, and they are always in opposite phases.
270^°, equivalent to a phase difference of 90^° in the opposite sense.
360^°, so the particles are in phase.

explanation:
The phase difference magnitude is


Δphi=(2piΔ x / lambda)
=(2pi(0.75) / 1)= (3pi / 2)=270^°.


A phase difference of 270^° is equivalent to -90^° modulo 360^°. Option B incorrectly treats three-quarters of a wavelength as half a wavelength.

title: Inferring wavelength from a particle-displacement graph
question: A displacement–distance graph shows two adjacent zero-displacement crossings at x=12 cm and x=30 cm. The curve crosses the equilibrium line in opposite directions at these two positions, with a crest between them. Adjacent equilibrium crossings enclosing one crest or one trough The wave speed is 330 m s^. What is its frequency?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 140" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M20 75 H300 M20 18 V120" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.2" fill="none" /><path d="M20 75 C42 75 42 30 65 30 S88 120 111 120 S134 30 157 30 S180 120 203 120 S226 30 249 30 S272 120 295 120" stroke="#2563eb" stroke-width="2.4" fill="none" /><path d="M65 30 V75 M111 120 V75 M157 30 V75" stroke="#64748b" stroke-dasharray="3 3" /><circle cx="65" cy="75" r="3.5" fill="#0D9488" /><circle cx="111" cy="75" r="3.5" fill="#0D9488" /><text x="65" y="91" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">12 cm</text><text x="111" y="105" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">30 cm</text><text x="160" y="135" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Horizontal axis: distance</text></svg>

options.text: 9.17 kHz
4.58 kHz

explanation:
1. Adjacent zero crossings enclose half a wavelength: lambda/2=30-12=18 cm.
2. Therefore lambda=36 cm=0.36 m.
3. f=v/lambda=330/0.36=916.7 Hz.

The options are inconsistent with the calculation. The correct answer is **916.7 Hz**; none of the listed options matches. The error in option A is a factor-of-ten mistake in interpreting the wavelength.

**Correction to Q22:** The correct frequency is 916.7 Hz. Replace option A with 916.7 Hz; the correct answer is then A.

title: Echo from a moving reflecting surface
question: A stationary sound source emits a short pulse towards a large reflecting wall. The wall moves directly away from the source at 5 m s^. Initially, the wall is 33 m from the source. Assume the speed of sound is 330 m s^. Wall receding from the stationary source Approximately how long after emission does the reflected sound return to the source?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 130" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><defs><marker id="a23" markerWidth="7" markerHeight="7" refX="5" refY="3" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L6,3 L0,6 Z" fill="#2563eb" /></marker></defs><circle cx="30" cy="58" r="9" fill="#0D9488" /><path d="M43 58 H245" stroke="#2563eb" stroke-width="2" marker-end="url(#a23)" /><path d="M258 20 V96" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="4" /><path d="M258 107 H303" stroke="#7C3AED" stroke-width="2" marker-end="url(#a23)" /><path d="M40 93 H258 M40 89 V97 M258 89 V97" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1" /><text x="30" y="41" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Source</text><text x="150" y="48" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Sound pulse</text><text x="155" y="86" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">33 m initially</text><text x="279" y="100" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Wall motion</text></svg>
explanation:
1. The sound reaches the moving wall after t₁=33/(330-5) is not correct, because the wall and sound approach each other? The sound moves towards the wall, which recedes; their closing speed is 330-5=325 m s^{-1}.
2. Thus t₁=33/325≈0.10154 s.
3. By then, the wall has moved 5(0.10154)≈0.508 m.
4. The return distance is 33+0.508=33.508 m, so the return time is 33.508/330≈0.10154 s.
5. Total time ≈0.20308 s.

The options are inconsistent. The correct result is approximately **0.203 s**; option A should be replaced with 0.203 s. This question illustrates why the wall's motion must be accounted for on both legs.

title: A megaphone and directional sound
question: A speaker is placed at the narrow end of a conical megaphone. The wide opening faces a listener. The sound rays are shown travelling outwards through the opening. A megaphone directs sound towards the audience Which explanation best describes the megaphone's action?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 130" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M25 50 L155 20 L155 100 L25 70 Z" fill="#94a3b8" fill-opacity="0.35" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" /><circle cx="28" cy="60" r="8" fill="#0D9488" /><path d="M155 20 L285 5 M155 60 H300 M155 100 L285 115" stroke="#2563eb" stroke-width="1.8" fill="none" /><path d="M275 1 L287 5 L277 11 M290 55 L302 60 L290 65 M275 109 L287 115 L275 119" stroke="#2563eb" stroke-width="1.5" fill="none" /><text x="85" y="14" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Megaphone</text><text x="25" y="88" text-anchor="middle" font-size="9" fill="currentColor">Source</text><text x="240" y="79" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Directed sound</text></svg>

options.text: It increases the frequency by compressing the sound waves.
It changes sound into electromagnetic waves, allowing them to travel farther.
It makes the sound longitudinal only inside the cone and transverse outside it.
Its walls reflect sound so that more acoustic energy is directed forwards, improving audibility in that direction.

explanation:
best describes the megaphone's action?

A) It increases the frequency by compressing the sound waves.

B) It changes sound into electromagnetic waves, allowing them to travel farther.

C) It makes the sound longitudinal only inside the cone and transverse outside it.

D) Its walls reflect sound so that more acoustic energy is directed forwards, improving audibility in that direction.

**Correct Answer: D**

**Reason:**

The conical walls reflect sound towards the opening, concentrating the sound energy in the forward direction. This improves audibility without changing the fundamental nature or frequency of the sound. Option A incorrectly assumes that reflection changes frequency.

title: Stethoscope: multiple reflections
question: A stethoscope has a chest piece, a narrow flexible tube and two earpieces. Sound from the patient's chest enters the chest piece and travels through the tube to the listener. Sound travels from the chest piece through the stethoscope tube Which principle is most directly responsible for helping the stethoscope convey weak body sounds to the listener?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 165" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="36" cy="45" r="17" fill="#94a3b8" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5" /><path d="M53 45 Q95 40 110 75 Q125 110 160 110 Q195 110 210 75 Q225 40 250 45" stroke="#2563eb" stroke-width="5" fill="none" stroke-linecap="round" /><path d="M250 45 L264 32 M250 45 L264 58" stroke="#2563eb" stroke-width="5" fill="none" stroke-linecap="round" /><path d="M264 32 V19 M264 58 V71" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="5" stroke-linecap="round" /><path d="M25 68 V90 H47 V68" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5" fill="none" /><text x="36" y="112" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Chest piece</text><text x="158" y="139" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Flexible tube</text><text x="276" y="91" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Earpieces</text><path d="M65 44 Q95 44 110 75" stroke="#0D9488" stroke-width="1.5" stroke-dasharray="3 3" fill="none" /></svg>

options.text: Sound undergoes repeated reflections within the tube, helping guide the sound towards the earpieces.
The tube creates new sound energy at every bend.
The sound frequency increases continuously as the sound moves through the tube.
The tube allows sound to travel without a medium.

explanation: The stethoscope provides a confined path in which sound can be transmitted to the ears, with reflections at the tube walls helping guide the sound. The chest piece also couples vibrations from the body into the instrument. Option B violates conservation of energy: the tube does not create sound energy.

title: Hearing range and ultrasonic frequency
question: A frequency scale shows three sources: P at 18 Hz, Q at 18,000 Hz, and R at 30,000 Hz. Assume a human audible range of approximately 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz. Frequency positions relative to the approximate human audible range Which classification is correct?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 120" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M25 55 H295" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" /><path d="M25 49 V61 M115 49 V61 M205 49 V61 M295 49 V61" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.3" /><circle cx="35" cy="55" r="5" fill="#7C3AED" /><circle cx="185" cy="55" r="5" fill="#0D9488" /><circle cx="260" cy="55" r="5" fill="#2563eb" /><text x="35" y="35" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">P: 18 Hz</text><text x="185" y="35" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Q: 18 kHz</text><text x="260" y="35" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">R: 30 kHz</text><text x="25" y="77" font-size="9" fill="currentColor">Low frequency</text><text x="295" y="77" text-anchor="end" font-size="9" fill="currentColor">High frequency</text><path d="M25 91 H205" stroke="#0D9488" stroke-width="5" /><path d="M205 91 H295" stroke="#2563eb" stroke-width="5" /><text x="115" y="108" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Approx. audible range</text><text x="252" y="108" text-anchor="middle" font-size="9" fill="currentColor">Ultrasound</text></svg>

options.text: P is ultrasonic, Q is infrasonic, and R is audible.
P is infrasonic, Q is audible, and R is ultrasonic.
P and R are both audible, while Q is ultrasonic.
All three are audible because they are mechanical waves.

explanation:
- P: 18 Hz<20 Hz, so it is infrasonic.
- Q: 20≤18,000≤20,000 Hz, so it is within the approximate audible range.
- R: 30,000 Hz>20,000 Hz, so it is ultrasonic.

Option D confuses the fact that sound is mechanical with the frequency limits of human hearing.

title: Damped vibrations and energy loss
question: A vibrating tuning fork is struck once. A microphone records its amplitude over time. The graph shows a gradually decreasing amplitude while the oscillations continue. Oscillations whose amplitude decreases with time Which statement correctly explains the graph?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 150" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M15 76 H305 M15 18 V132" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.2" fill="none" /><path d="M15 76 C23 15 31 15 39 76 S55 115 63 76 S79 43 87 76 S103 98 111 76 S127 59 135 76 S151 87 159 76 S175 67 183 76 S199 82 207 76 S223 71 231 76 S247 79 255 76 S271 73 279 76 S295 77 305 76" stroke="#2563eb" stroke-width="2" fill="none" /><path d="M15 76 Q55 8 95 76 T175 76 T255 76 T305 76" stroke="#64748b" stroke-width="0.8" stroke-dasharray="3 3" fill="none" /><path d="M15 76 Q55 144 95 76 T175 76 T255 76 T305 76" stroke="#64748b" stroke-width="0.8" stroke-dasharray="3 3" fill="none" /><text x="11" y="12" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Amplitude</text><text x="302" y="94" text-anchor="end" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Time →</text><text x="160" y="145" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Decreasing amplitude</text></svg>

options.text: The frequency must decrease to zero immediately, while the amplitude remains constant.
The tuning fork undergoes resonance because its amplitude is decreasing.
The vibration is damped; energy is transferred to the surroundings, so the amplitude decreases.
The graph represents free vibrations without any energy loss.

explanation: Damping occurs when energy is lost from the oscillating system, for example through air resistance and sound radiation. The amplitude therefore decreases with time. Option D describes an ideal undamped system, whose amplitude would remain constant.

title: Forced vibration versus resonance
question: A vibrating driver is connected to a second mechanical system. The driver frequency can be varied. The graph shows the steady-state amplitude of the second system against the driving frequency, with a sharp maximum at f₀. Amplitude response as driving frequency is varied Which statement is correct at frequencies away from f₀, provided the driver continues operating?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 160" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M32 15 V130 H300" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.2" fill="none" /><path d="M45 121 C85 119 104 112 123 88 S148 25 174 25 S203 88 223 108 S265 121 295 123" stroke="#0D9488" stroke-width="2.5" fill="none" /><path d="M174 25 V130" stroke="#64748b" stroke-dasharray="4 4" /><text x="174" y="16" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">f₀</text><text x="13" y="18" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">A</text><text x="299" y="146" text-anchor="end" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Driving frequency</text><text x="174" y="154" text-anchor="middle" font-size="9" fill="currentColor">Natural frequency</text></svg>

options.text: The system can undergo forced vibrations, but its amplitude is generally smaller than at resonance.
The system must stop vibrating because forced vibrations occur only at resonance.
The system undergoes free vibrations at the driver's frequency.
The system must vibrate with infinite amplitude at every frequency.

explanation: Forced vibrations occur whenever a system is driven periodically. Resonance is the special condition in which the driving frequency matches or is close to the natural frequency, producing a maximum response. Option B incorrectly treats forced vibration and resonance as identical phenomena.

title: Resonance tube and end correction
question: A closed resonance tube produces two successive resonances at air-column lengths 16 cm and 50 cm. The open end is not perfectly at the displacement antinode; its end correction is e. Successive resonances in a tube closed by water If the speed of sound is 340 m s^, what is the frequency of the sound?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 160" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M48 18 V130 M82 18 V130" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2.5" fill="none" /><path d="M50 96 H80 V128 H50 Z" fill="#60A5FA" fill-opacity="0.65" /><path d="M50 96 H80" stroke="#2563eb" stroke-width="2" /><path d="M98 18 V96 M93 18 H103 M93 96 H103" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1" /><text x="109" y="61" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">L₁ = 16 cm</text><path d="M210 18 V130 M244 18 V130" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2.5" fill="none" /><path d="M212 116 H242 V128 H212 Z" fill="#60A5FA" fill-opacity="0.65" /><path d="M212 116 H242" stroke="#2563eb" stroke-width="2" /><path d="M260 18 V116 M255 18 H265 M255 116 H265" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1" /><text x="270" y="70" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">50 cm</text><text x="65" y="145" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">First</text><text x="227" y="145" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Second</text></svg>

options.text: 500 Hz
250 Hz
125 Hz

explanation:
1. Successive resonance lengths differ by half a wavelength: lambda/2=50-16=34 cm.
2. Thus lambda=68 cm=0.68 m.
3. f=v/lambda=340/0.68=500 Hz.

The end correction cancels when taking the difference between successive resonance lengths. Option B incorrectly uses the difference in lengths as a full wavelength.

title: Fundamental frequency of an open pipe versus a closed pipe
question: Two pipes of equal physical length L are shown. Pipe P is open at both ends, whereas pipe Q is closed at one end and open at the other. End correction is neglected for this idealised comparison. Open and closed pipes of equal length What is the ratio f_/f_ of their fundamental frequencies?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 145" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><text x="10" y="22" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">P: Open pipe</text><path d="M35 35 H285 M35 55 H285" stroke="#0D9488" stroke-width="3" /><path d="M35 35 V55 M285 35 V55" stroke="#0D9488" stroke-width="1.5" stroke-dasharray="3 3" /><text x="160" y="48" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">L</text><text x="10" y="83" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Q: Closed pipe</text><path d="M35 96 V122 H285 V96" stroke="#2563eb" stroke-width="3" fill="none" /><path d="M35 96 V122" stroke="#2563eb" stroke-width="5" /><text x="160" y="115" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">L</text><text x="160" y="141" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Equal physical lengths</text></svg>
explanation:
For an open pipe, the fundamental wavelength is lambda_o=2L, so f_o=v/(2L).

For a closed pipe, the fundamental wavelength is lambda_c=4L, so f_c=v/(4L).

Therefore,


(f_c / f_o)=(v/(4L) / v/(2L))=frac12.


Option C incorrectly assumes that equal pipe lengths always produce equal fundamental frequencies, regardless of the end conditions.

question: An experiment records the following data for three sound waves travelling in the same medium. | **Wave** | **Frequency** | **Wavelength** | | P | 220 Hz | 1.50 m | | Q | 330 Hz | 1.00 m | | R | 440 Hz |? | Experimental data for waves in a common medium Which wavelength for R makes the data physically consistent?

title: Determining the wave speed from a waveform and a frequency meter
question: A wave generator produces sound. The oscilloscope trace shows a period of 2.5 ms, while a spatial sensor measures a wavelength of 0.825 m. Time-domain trace and independently measured wavelength What is the wave speed?
diagramSvg:
<svg viewBox="0 0 460 190" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="background:#f8fafc; border-radius:8px; border:1px solid #cbd5e1; font-family:system-ui, sans-serif;">

        <line x1="0" y1="35" x2="170" y2="35" stroke="#cbd5e1"/>
        <path d="M 0 35 Q 20 15 40 35 T 80 35 T 120 35 T 160 35" fill="none" stroke="#2563eb" stroke-width="2"/>
        <text x="85" y="60" text-anchor="middle" font-size="9.5" font-weight="700" fill="#1e40af">Small Amplitude → Faint Sound</text>
      </g>
      <!-- Wave 2 (Loud Note - Same Pitch) -->
      <g transform="translate(240, 45)">
        <line x1="0" y1="35" x2="170" y2="35" stroke="#cbd5e1"/>
        <path d="M 0 35 Q 20 -5 40 35 T 80 35 T 120 35 T 160 35" fill="none" stroke="#dc2626" stroke-width="2.5"/>
        <text x="85" y="60" text-anchor="middle" font-size="9.5" font-weight="700" fill="#991b1b">Large Amplitude → Loud Sound</text>
      </g>
      <rect x="50" y="125" width="360" height="42" rx="4" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#cbd5e1"/>
      <text x="230" y="142" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" font-weight="700" fill="#1e293b">• Loudness depends on (Amplitude)²</text>
      <text x="230" y="156" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" font-weight="700" fill="#1e293b">• Pitch depends on Frequency | Quality depends on Waveform</text>
    </svg>
explanation:
The period is T=2.5×10^{-3} s.


f=frac1T=frac1{0.0025}=400 Hz.


Then


v=flambda=400×0.825=330 m s^{-1}.


The correct answer is **A**, not D. Option D is twice the correct value, a common error from confusing the full period with half a period.

title: Distinguishing amplitude from loudness in a waveform
question: A microphone records two tones of the same frequency. The first waveform has an amplitude of 1 mm, while the second has an amplitude of 3 mm. Both are recorded with the same microphone under the same conditions. Same frequency, different amplitudes Under otherwise identical conditions, what is the ratio of the sound intensities I_Q/I_P?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 75" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M12 38 H308" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="0.6" /><path d="M12 38 C32 18 52 18 72 38 S112 58 132 38 S172 18 192 38 S232 58 252 38 S292 18 308 38" stroke="#0D9488" stroke-width="2" fill="none" /><text x="16" y="12" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Tone P: A = 1 mm</text></svg>
explanation:
Sound intensity is proportional to the square of amplitude for otherwise comparable waves:


(I_Q / I_P)=≤ft((A_Q / A_P)right)²
=≤ft(frac31right)²=9.


Option A assumes intensity is directly proportional to amplitude rather than amplitude squared.

        <text x="85" y="60" text-anchor="middle" font-size="9.5" font-weight="700" fill="#991b1b">Large Amplitude → Loud Sound</text>

      <rect x="50" y="125" width="360" height="42" rx="4" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#cbd5e1"/>
      <text x="230" y="142" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" font-weight="700" fill="#1e293b">• Loudness depends on (Amplitude)²</text>
      <text x="230" y="156" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" font-weight="700" fill="#1e293b">• Pitch depends on Frequency | Quality depends on Waveform</text>
    </svg>

options.text: Pressure is maximum in Q and S and minimum in P and R.
Pressure is equal everywhere because the particles move longitudinally.
Pressure is minimum in P and R and maximum in Q and S.
Pressure is maximum in P and R and minimum in Q and S.

explanation: Compressions are regions of high particle density and pressure; rarefactions are regions of low density and pressure. Therefore P and R have higher pressure, while Q and S have lower pressure. Option A reverses the two regions.

title: Inferring frequency from two wavefront diagrams
question: Two wavefront diagrams show sound emitted by two sources in the same medium. During the same time interval, source P produces four complete cycles, while source Q produces six complete cycles. Their amplitudes are equal. Wavefronts produced in equal observation intervals If P has a frequency of 200 Hz, what is the frequency of Q?
diagramSvg:
<svg viewBox="0 0 460 190" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="background:#f8fafc; border-radius:8px; border:1px solid #cbd5e1; font-family:system-ui, sans-serif;">
      <text x="230" y="24" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13" font-weight="700" fill="#0f172a">Waveforms: Pitch, Loudness & Quality (Timbre)</text>
      <!-- Wave 1 (Soft Note) -->
      <g transform="translate(40, 45)">
        <line x1="0" y1="35" x2="170" y2="35" stroke="#cbd5e1"/>
        <path d="M 0 35 Q 20 15 40 35 T 80 35 T 120 35 T 160 35" fill="none" stroke="#2563eb" stroke-width="2"/>
        <text x="85" y="60" text-anchor="middle" font-size="9.5" font-weight="700" fill="#1e40af">Small Amplitude → Faint Sound</text>
      </g>
      <!-- Wave 2 (Loud Note - Same Pitch) -->
      <g transform="translate(240, 45)">
        <line x1="0" y1="35" x2="170" y2="35" stroke="#cbd5e1"/>
        <path d="M 0 35 Q 20 -5 40 35 T 80 35 T 120 35 T 160 35" fill="none" stroke="#dc2626" stroke-width="2.5"/>
        <text x="85" y="60" text-anchor="middle" font-size="9.5" font-weight="700" fill="#991b1b">Large Amplitude → Loud Sound</text>
      </g>
