    </svg>

options.text: 200 Hz
300 Hz
400 Hz

explanation:
Frequency is the number of complete cycles per second. In equal time intervals, the frequency ratio is the ratio of the number of cycles:


(f_Q / f_P)=frac64=frac32.


Thus f_Q=200×3/2=300 Hz. Equal amplitudes do not imply equal frequencies, which is the trap in option B.

title: Resonance in a sonometer using a tuning fork
question: A vibrating tuning fork is held above a sonometer wire. A small paper rider rests on the wire. The wire tension is adjusted until the rider is thrown off most vigorously, indicating resonance between the fork and the wire's fundamental mode. Resonance between a tuning fork and a sonometer wire Which observation most strongly indicates that resonance has occurred?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 155" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M70 20 V50 Q70 60 80 60 Q90 60 90 50 V20 M70 20 V8 M90 20 V8" stroke="#7C3AED" stroke-width="4" fill="none" stroke-linecap="round" /><path d="M80 60 V70" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" /><path d="M35 110 H275" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" /><path d="M52 92 L62 110 L42 110 Z M248 92 L258 110 L238 110 Z" fill="#64748b" /><path d="M62 110 H248" stroke="#0D9488" stroke-width="2.5" /><path d="M155 110 V89" stroke="#2563eb" stroke-width="1.5" /><path d="M149 89 H161 L155 82 Z" fill="#2563eb" /><text x="80" y="79" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Tuning fork</text><text x="155" y="75" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Paper rider</text><text x="160" y="135" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Sonometer wire</text><text x="160" y="149" text-anchor="middle" font-size="9" fill="currentColor">Tension adjusted to obtain resonance</text></svg>

options.text: The paper rider is thrown off when the wire's natural frequency matches the tuning fork's frequency.
The wire stops vibrating because the tuning fork absorbs its energy.
The wire vibrates most strongly when its natural frequency is unrelated to the tuning fork's frequency.
The tuning fork's frequency increases until it matches the wire automatically.

explanation: At resonance, the driving frequency matches the wire's natural frequency, producing a large vibration amplitude. The rider may be thrown off as a result. Option C describes a frequency mismatch, which generally produces a smaller response.

title: Open pipe: identifying the second harmonic
question: An open pipe is shown with a standing-wave pattern containing two half-wavelength segments. Both ends are displacement antinodes, and there is a displacement node at the centre. Second harmonic of an open pipe If the speed of sound is 330 m s^, what is the frequency of the pattern?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 125" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M25 28 H295 M25 48 H295" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" /><path d="M25 38 Q58 0 92 38 T160 38 T228 38 T295 38" stroke="#0D9488" stroke-width="2.5" fill="none" /><path d="M25 19 V56 M160 19 V56 M295 19 V56" stroke="#64748b" stroke-dasharray="3 3" /><text x="25" y="69" text-anchor="middle" font-size="9" fill="currentColor">Antinode</text><text x="160" y="69" text-anchor="middle" font-size="9" fill="currentColor">Node</text><text x="295" y="69" text-anchor="middle" font-size="9" fill="currentColor">Antinode</text><text x="160" y="95" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">L = 0.60 m</text><text x="160" y="112" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Two half-wavelength segments</text></svg>

options.text: 275 Hz
550 Hz

explanation:
For an open pipe in the second harmonic,


L=(2lambda / 2)=lambda.


Thus lambda=0.60 m, and


f=(330 / 0.60)=550 Hz.


The fundamental frequency is 330/(2×0.60)=275 Hz, so option B is the fundamental rather than the second harmonic.

title: Closed pipe: why even harmonics are absent
question: A closed pipe has a displacement node at its closed end and a displacement antinode at its open end. Three possible standing-wave patterns are proposed: P has one quarter-wavelength, Q has two quarter-wavelengths, and R has three quarter-wavelengths. Candidate standing-wave patterns in a pipe closed at one end Which pattern is physically allowed for a closed pipe, based on the boundary conditions?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 165" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><text x="8" y="25" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">P</text><path d="M30 15 V45 H290 V15" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5" fill="none" /><path d="M30 30 Q160 0 290 30" stroke="#0D9488" stroke-width="2" fill="none" /><text x="8" y="77" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Q</text><path d="M30 65 V95 H290 V65" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5" fill="none" /><path d="M30 80 Q95 50 160 80 T290 80" stroke="#2563eb" stroke-width="2" fill="none" /><text x="8" y="129" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">R</text><path d="M30 115 V145 H290 V115" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5" fill="none" /><path d="M30 130 Q73 100 116 130 T203 130 T290 130" stroke="#7C3AED" stroke-width="2" fill="none" /><text x="160" y="160" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Closed end at left; open end at right</text></svg>

options.text: Only Q, because a closed pipe supports only even harmonics.
P and R, corresponding to the first and third allowed harmonics.
P, Q and R, because every harmonic is allowed in every pipe.
Only Q and R, because the fundamental is absent in a closed pipe.

explanation:
A closed pipe requires a displacement node at the closed end and an antinode at the open end. Its allowed lengths are odd multiples of a quarter-wavelength:


L=(lambda / 4),quad(3lambda / 4),quad(5lambda / 4),ldots


Thus the first and third harmonics are allowed, while even harmonics are absent. Option A reverses the harmonic rule.

title: Estimating the speed of sound from echo measurements
question: A student stands at three known distances from a large wall and records the echo-return time for each trial. The data are plotted below. Echo-return time increases with source-to-wall distance If the wall distance is 82.5 m when the echo returns after 0.50 s, what speed of sound is inferred?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 165" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M38 15 V132 H300" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.2" fill="none" /><path d="M38 132 L300 15" stroke="#64748b" stroke-width="0.8" stroke-dasharray="3 3" /><circle cx="82" cy="112" r="4" fill="#0D9488" /><circle cx="148" cy="80" r="4" fill="#0D9488" /><circle cx="214" cy="48" r="4" fill="#0D9488" /><path d="M82 112 L148 80 L214 48" stroke="#0D9488" stroke-width="2" fill="none" /><text x="82" y="126" text-anchor="middle" font-size="9" fill="currentColor">0.5 s</text><text x="148" y="94" text-anchor="middle" font-size="9" fill="currentColor">1.0 s</text><text x="214" y="62" text-anchor="middle" font-size="9" fill="currentColor">1.5 s</text><text x="160" y="151" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Distance from wall</text><text x="12" y="18" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Echo time</text></svg>
explanation:
The echo covers the round-trip distance:


d_{total}=2(82.5)=165 m.


Therefore,


v=(165 / 0.50)=330 m s^{-1}.


Option A uses the one-way distance rather than the full distance travelled by the sound.

title: String vibration: simultaneous changes in length, tension and linear density
question: A sonometer wire is adjusted from state P to state Q. In P, the vibrating length is L, tension is T, and linear density is µ. In Q, the length becomes 2L, tension becomes 8T, and linear density becomes 2µ. One string with three changed parameters What is the ratio f_Q/f_P?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 155" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><text x="12" y="18" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">State P</text><path d="M30 40 H140" stroke="#0D9488" stroke-width="2.5" /><path d="M30 33 V47 M140 33 V47" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5" /><text x="85" y="61" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">L, T, μ</text><text x="12" y="87" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">State Q</text><path d="M30 109 H250" stroke="#2563eb" stroke-width="2.5" /><path d="M30 102 V116 M250 102 V116" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5" /><text x="140" y="131" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">2L, 8T, 2μ</text><text x="160" y="149" text-anchor="middle" font-size="9" fill="currentColor">Fundamental mode in both states</text></svg>
explanation:
For a stretched string,


f=(1 / 2L)√((T / µ)).


Hence,


(f_Q / f_P)
=(L / 2L)
√((8T/(2µ) / T/µ))
=frac12sqrt4=1.


The frequency remains unchanged because the doubling of length is exactly offset by the increase in √(T/µ). Option B accounts for tension but neglects both length and linear density.

title: Finding a missing value from a sound-wave experiment
question: An experiment records the following data for three sound waves travelling in the same medium. Which wavelength for R makes the data physically consistent?
diagramSvg: <svg viewBox="0 0 460 158" width="100%" class="q-diagram-svg" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="15" y="10" width="430" height="138" rx="6" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#cbd5e1" stroke-width="1.5"/><rect x="15" y="10" width="430" height="37" rx="6" fill="#f1f5f9"/><line x1="15" y1="47" x2="445" y2="47" stroke="#cbd5e1" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="30" y="39" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="bold" fill="#1e293b">**Wave**</text><text x="170" y="39" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="bold" fill="#1e293b">**Frequency**</text><text x="310" y="39" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="bold" fill="#1e293b">**Wavelength**</text><rect x="16" y="52" width="428" height="32" fill="#fafafa"/><text x="30" y="71" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="normal" fill="#334155">P</text><text x="170" y="71" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="normal" fill="#334155">220 Hz</text><text x="310" y="71" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="normal" fill="#334155">1.50 m</text><text x="30" y="103" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="normal" fill="#334155">Q</text><text x="170" y="103" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="normal" fill="#334155">330 Hz</text><text x="310" y="103" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="normal" fill="#334155">1.00 m</text><rect x="16" y="116" width="428" height="32" fill="#fafafa"/><text x="30" y="135" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="normal" fill="#334155">R</text><text x="170" y="135" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="normal" fill="#334155">440 Hz</text><text x="310" y="135" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="normal" fill="#334155">?</text></svg>
explanation:
1. Wave P gives v=220×1.50=330 m s^{-1}.
2. Wave Q gives v=330×1.00=330 m s^{-1}, confirming the common speed.
3. For R, lambda=v/f=330/440=0.75 m.

The options are inconsistent. The correct wavelength is **0.75 m**, so option B should be the correct answer. This checks whether the constant wave speed in a common medium is applied consistently.

title: Sound waves versus light waves
question: The upper diagram shows a sound wave travelling through air, represented by alternating compressions and rarefactions. The lower diagram represents a light wave travelling through vacuum, with mutually perpendicular electric and magnetic fields. Which conclusion follows from the physical nature of these two waves?

<svg viewBox="0 0 460 190" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="background:#f8fafc; border-radius:8px; border:1px solid #cbd5e1; font-family:system-ui, sans-serif;">

      </g>
      <!-- Wave 2 (Loud Note - Same Pitch) -->
      <g transform="translate(240, 45)">
        <line x1="0" y1="35" x2="170" y2="35" stroke="#cbd5e1"/>

      <text x="230" y="142" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" font-weight="700" fill="#1e293b">• Loudness depends on (Amplitude)²</text>

options.text: Both waves require a material medium because all waves are mechanical.
Sound can travel through a vacuum if its frequency is sufficiently high.
Light is longitudinal because its electric and magnetic fields are perpendicular to each other.
Sound in air is longitudinal and mechanical, whereas light is transverse and electromagnetic; only sound requires a material medium.

explanation:
1. Sound propagates through air by longitudinal pressure variations and requires a material medium.
2. Light is an electromagnetic wave and can travel through a vacuum.
3. The electric and magnetic fields of light are perpendicular to the direction of propagation, which is consistent with a transverse wave. Option C confuses perpendicular electric and magnetic fields with longitudinal propagation.

title: Distinguishing musical quality or timbre
question: Three sound waveforms, P, Q and R, are recorded over the same time interval. All three have the same fundamental frequency and the same maximum displacement, but their waveform shapes differ because their harmonic compositions differ. Which statement is correct?
diagramSvg:
<svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 80" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg">
    <path d="M10 40 H310" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="0.7"/>
    <path d="M10 40 C25 5 45 5 60 40 S95 75 110 40 S145 5 160 40 S195 75 210 40 S245 5 260 40 S295 75 310 40" stroke="#0D9488" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/>
    <text x="14" y="13" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">P</text>
  </svg>

options.text: The sounds must have different pitches because their waveforms have different shapes.
The sounds can have the same pitch and, under the stated conditions, the same amplitude, but different quality because their harmonic compositions differ.
The sounds must have different speeds because their amplitudes are equal.
The sounds must have different fundamental frequencies because their waveforms are not identical.

explanation:
1. Pitch is primarily determined by the fundamental frequency. Since the fundamental frequencies are equal, the perceived pitches can be the same.
2. The maximum displacement is the same, so the amplitudes are equal.
3. The differing waveforms indicate different harmonic compositions, producing different timbres or qualities.
4. Option A confuses waveform shape, which influences quality, with fundamental frequency, which primarily determines pitch.

title: Interpreting a displacement–distance graph
question: The graph below represents the displacement of particles in a medium at a particular instant. The horizontal axis represents distance along the direction of propagation, and the vertical axis represents particle displacement. Displacement–distance graph at one instant If the wave travels at 330 m s^ and the horizontal separation between two consecutive crests is 0.75 m, which statement is correct?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 190" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><defs><marker id="arr1" markerWidth="7" markerHeight="7" refX="5" refY="3" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L6,3 L0,6 Z" fill="currentColor" /></marker></defs><path d="M32 92 H300 M32 162 V15" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.4" fill="none" marker-end="url(#arr1)" /><path d="M32 92 H300" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="0.6" stroke-dasharray="3 3" /><path d="M32 92 C52 92 52 32 82 32 S112 152 142 152 S172 32 202 32 S232 152 262 152 S292 92 300 92" stroke="#0D9488" stroke-width="2.5" fill="none" /><path d="M82 32 V92 M202 32 V92" stroke="#64748b" stroke-dasharray="4 3" /><path d="M82 25 H202" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1" /><text x="142" y="18" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">λ</text><text x="10" y="18" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">y</text><text x="300" y="108" text-anchor="end" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Distance x</text><text x="22" y="96" text-anchor="end" font-size="9" fill="currentColor">0</text><text x="87" y="104" font-size="9" fill="currentColor">Crest</text><text x="145" y="146" font-size="9" fill="currentColor">Trough</text></svg>

options.text: The frequency is 247.5 Hz, and the graph directly gives the time period.
The frequency is 440 Hz, and the graph gives the amplitude but not the wavelength.
The frequency is 440 Hz, and the graph gives the wavelength but not the time period directly.
The frequency is 0.00227 Hz, because the wavelength must be divided by the speed.

explanation:
1. The distance between consecutive crests is one wavelength: lambda=0.75 m.
2. Using v=flambda, f=330/0.75=440 Hz.
3. The graph is a spatial snapshot, so it does not directly provide the time period. The tempting mistake in B is to confuse the graph's wavelength information with the absence of amplitude information: the vertical displacement does show amplitude.

title: Displacement–time graph and particle motion
question: A particle of the medium oscillates according to the graph shown. The horizontal axis is time, and one complete cycle takes 4 ms. Displacement–time graph of a vibrating particle Which combination correctly identifies the frequency and the particle's state after 1 ms, assuming the cycle begins at zero displacement moving towards positive displacement?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 180" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M28 88 H300 M28 150 V14" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.3" fill="none" /><path d="M28 88 C48 88 48 32 78 32 S108 144 138 144 S168 32 198 32 S228 144 258 144 S288 88 300 88" stroke="#2563eb" stroke-width="2.5" fill="none" /><path d="M28 32 H300 M28 144 H300" stroke="#64748b" stroke-dasharray="3 4" stroke-width="0.7" /><text x="9" y="20" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">y</text><text x="300" y="103" text-anchor="end" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">t (ms)</text><text x="78" y="24" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">+A</text><text x="138" y="158" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">−A</text><text x="78" y="105" text-anchor="middle" font-size="9" fill="currentColor">1</text><text x="198" y="105" text-anchor="middle" font-size="9" fill="currentColor">3</text><text x="258" y="105" text-anchor="middle" font-size="9" fill="currentColor">4</text><path d="M78 166 H258" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1" /><path d="M78 162 V170 M258 162 V170" stroke="currentColor" /><text x="168" y="178" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">One period = 4 ms</text></svg>

options.text: 250 Hz; maximum positive displacement.
250 Hz; zero displacement moving towards negative displacement.
4 Hz; maximum negative displacement.
1000 Hz; zero displacement moving towards positive displacement.

explanation:
1. T=4 ms=0.004 s.
2. f=1/T=1/0.004=250 Hz.
3. After one-quarter period, t=T/4=1 ms, the particle reaches maximum positive displacement. Option C confuses the period measured in milliseconds with the frequency in hertz.

title: Distinguishing amplitude from wavelength
question: Two waves travel through the same medium at the same speed. Wave P has a crest height of 2 cm and a crest-to-crest distance of 60 cm. Wave Q has a crest height of 4 cm and a crest-to-crest distance of 60 cm. Schematic comparison; both waves have the same wavelength If the waves carry sound and all other relevant conditions are identical, which inference is justified?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 100" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M15 52 H305" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="0.8" /><path d="M15 52 Q30 12 45 52 T75 52 T105 52 T135 52 T165 52 T195 52 T225 52 T255 52 T285 52" stroke="#0D9488" stroke-width="2" fill="none" /><path d="M45 52 V14 M45 14 H62" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="0.8" /><text x="66" y="18" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">2 cm</text><text x="160" y="92" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Wave P: λ = 60 cm</text></svg>

options.text: Q has twice the frequency and twice the speed of P.
Q has twice the frequency but the same amplitude as P.
Q has half the frequency and four times the intensity of P.
Q has the same frequency and speed as P, but its intensity is four times that of P under the usual intensity–amplitude relation.

explanation:
1. The wavelengths are equal, and both waves travel in the same medium, so their speeds are equal.
2. From v=flambda, equal speeds and wavelengths imply equal frequencies.
3. For a sound wave under the same conditions, intensity is proportional to amplitude squared: Ipropto A².
4. Doubling the amplitude gives I_Q/I_P=(4/2)²=4. Option A incorrectly assumes that amplitude determines frequency.

title: Identifying compressions and rarefactions
question: A longitudinal sound wave travels from left to right through air. The dots represent air particles at a particular instant. Alternating regions of high and low particle density The distance between the centres of C₁ and C₂ is 0.90 m. If the frequency is 550 Hz, which statement is correct?
diagramSvg:
<svg viewBox="0 0 460 190" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="background:#f8fafc; border-radius:8px; border:1px solid #cbd5e1; font-family:system-ui, sans-serif;">
      <text x="230" y="24" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13" font-weight="700" fill="#0f172a">Waveforms: Pitch, Loudness & Quality (Timbre)</text>
      <!-- Wave 1 (Soft Note) -->
      <g transform="translate(40, 45)">
        <line x1="0" y1="35" x2="170" y2="35" stroke="#cbd5e1"/>
        <path d="M 0 35 Q 20 15 40 35 T 80 35 T 120 35 T 160 35" fill="none" stroke="#2563eb" stroke-width="2"/>
        <text x="85" y="60" text-anchor="middle" font-size="9.5" font-weight="700" fill="#1e40af">Small Amplitude → Faint Sound</text>
      </g>

question: A student stands in front of a rigid wall. The sound travels from the student to the wall and back. The time between producing the sound and hearing its echo must be at least 0.1 s for the echo to be heard distinctly. The echo travels twice the separation between the student and the wall Using the prescribed speed of sound of 330 m s^, what is the minimum separation required?

title: Resonance tube: first and second resonances
question: A resonance tube is closed at the lower end by water and open at the upper end. As the water level is lowered, the first loud resonance occurs when the air-column length is 17 cm, and the next loud resonance occurs when it is 51 cm. Closed air column with two successive resonance lengths Ignoring measurement error, what is the wavelength of the sound and the end correction?

explanation:
1. Successive resonances in a closed tube differ by lambda/2.

title: Harmonics in an open pipe
question: An open organ pipe is shown with both ends open. The diagram shows the third harmonic as three half-wavelength segments fitting inside the pipe. Third harmonic of an open pipe: three half-wavelength segments If the speed of sound is 330 m s^, what is the frequency of the third harmonic?

110 Hz

explanation:
1. For an open pipe, L=nlambda_n/2.
2. For the third harmonic, n=3, so lambda₃=2L/3=2(0.90)/3=0.60 m.
3. f₃=330/0.60=550 Hz.
4. Option A is the fundamental frequency divided by three, rather than multiplied by three.

title: Harmonics in a closed pipe
question: A pipe is closed at one end and open at the other. The standing-wave diagram shows the third allowed mode, with three quarter-wavelength segments inside the tube. Closed pipe: only odd harmonics are allowed If the speed of sound is 330 m s^, what is the frequency of this mode?

330 Hz
550 Hz
660 Hz

explanation:
1. In a closed pipe, allowed harmonics are 1,3,5,ldots.
2. The third allowed mode is the fifth harmonic: L=5lambda/4.
3. lambda=4L/5=4(0.75)/5=0.60 m.
4. f=330/0.60=550 Hz. Option B would correspond to the third harmonic, not the fifth.

title: Sonometer: tension and frequency
question: A sonometer wire of fixed length L and fixed linear density µ is stretched over two bridges. A movable mass applies tension T. A paper rider rests at the centre of the wire. Sonometer wire with fixed vibrating length and adjustable tension The tension is increased from T to 4T, while the wire's length and mass per unit length remain unchanged. What happens to its fundamental frequency?

options.text: It doubles, because fpropto√(T).
It becomes four times as large, because frequency is directly proportional to tension.
It halves, because increased tension increases the wavelength.
It remains unchanged because the vibrating length is fixed.

explanation:
For a stretched string,


f=(1 / 2L)√((T / µ)).


Therefore,


(f₂ / f₁)=√((4T / T))=2.

title: Sonar and the depth of the sea
question: A ship sends an ultrasonic pulse vertically downwards. The pulse reflects from the seabed and returns to the receiver on the ship after 2.4 s. The speed of sound in seawater is 1500 m s^. Ultrasonic pulse travelling to the seabed and back Which conclusion is correct?

options.text: The depth is 3600 m, because the full distance is vt.
The depth is 1800 m, because the measured time includes the downward and upward journeys.

The depth is 1500/2.4=625 m, because distance is speed divided by time.

explanation:
1. Total distance travelled by the pulse is 1500×2.4=3600 m.
2. The depth is half the round-trip distance: 3600/2=1800 m.

title: Sound board behind a speaker
question: Two identical sound sources are placed in front of two listeners. Source P has a concave sound-reflecting board behind it, directing more sound towards the listener. Source Q has no board. The board can direct more sound energy towards the listener, increasing sound intensity in that direction without changing the source frequency.
The board converts longitudinal sound waves into transverse waves.

explanation: A sound board reflects and directs sound towards the audience, improving audibility in the desired direction. It does not create energy or change the frequency emitted by the source. Option B confuses concentration of sound energy with creation of energy.

title: Comparing frequencies of two vibrating strings
question: Two stretched strings have the same material and are vibrating in their fundamental modes. String P has length L, tension T, and linear density µ. String Q has length 2L, tension 4T, and linear density 2µ. Fundamental vibrations of strings with different lengths, tensions and linear densities What is the ratio f_Q/f_P?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 150" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><text x="15" y="20" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">String P</text><path d="M30 48 H150" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" /><path d="M30 48 Q90 8 150 48" stroke="#0D9488" stroke-width="2.5" fill="none" /><text x="90" y="70" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">L, T, μ</text><text x="15" y="93" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">String Q</text><path d="M30 120 H270" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" /><path d="M30 120 Q150 80 270 120" stroke="#7C3AED" stroke-width="2.5" fill="none" /><text x="150" y="143" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">2L, 4T, 2μ</text></svg>

For a stretched string,


f=(1 / 2L)√((T / µ)).


Thus,


(f_Q / f_P)
=(L / 2L)√((4T/(2µ) / T/µ))
=frac12sqrt2.


The calculated ratio is 1/sqrt2, which is not among the options. The correct ratio is **1/sqrt2**; the options must be corrected before this question is used. The trap is to compare tension alone and ignore both length and linear density.

**Correction to Q15:** Replace option A with 1/sqrt2. The correct answer is A after this correction.

options.text: The increase occurs because warmer air necessarily has a greater density.
The speed increases because the sound frequency increases automatically with temperature.
The speed increases because sound travels faster in warmer air; for a fixed source frequency, its wavelength consequently increases.
The speed increases only if atmospheric pressure increases.

explanation:
1. At ordinary temperatures, sound travels faster in warmer air because the molecular properties governing propagation change with temperature.
2. For a fixed source, frequency remains constant.
3. Since v=flambda, an increase in v at constant f means an increase in lambda. Option B incorrectly assumes the medium automatically changes the source frequency.

title: Humidity and sound propagation
question: Two identical sound sources are placed at equal distances from two microphones. One path passes through relatively dry air; the other passes through humid air. Temperature and pressure are held constant. Comparison of sound propagation through dry and humid air Which statement best describes the expected effect of humidity on the speed of sound in air?

options.text: Humid air generally allows sound to travel faster than dry air at the same temperature and pressure, because humid air is less dense.
Humidity always halves the speed of sound because water vapour absorbs half the energy.
Humidity changes the frequency emitted by the source, which necessarily changes the speed.
Humidity has exactly the same effect as doubling the sound frequency.

explanation: At the same temperature and pressure, humid air is generally less dense than dry air because water vapour has a lower molar mass than the average dry-air mixture. The speed of sound is therefore generally slightly higher in humid air. Option C confuses a change in propagation conditions with a change in the source frequency.

title: Free vibrations versus forced vibrations
question: A tuning fork is struck and brought near a second tuning fork mounted on a stand. The second fork is initially at rest and begins to vibrate due to the periodic sound waves from the first fork. One tuning fork drives the vibrations of another through air Which description is correct for the second tuning fork?

options.text: It undergoes free vibrations because no direct contact occurs between the forks.
It undergoes forced vibrations and may reach a large amplitude because its natural frequency matches the driving frequency.
It undergoes damped vibrations only, since every sound wave removes all energy immediately.
It remains at rest because sound cannot transfer energy without physical contact.

explanation:
1. The sound waves exert a periodic driving influence on the second fork.
2. Its motion is therefore forced, not free.
3. Since the driving frequency matches its natural frequency, resonance can produce a comparatively large amplitude. Option A incorrectly assumes that forced vibrations require direct physical contact.
